This is the first-ever public confirmation of zero-click mercenary spyware delivered via targeted ads. We call the technique AdFection, and show how it was used to infect devices at Al Jazeera with Candiru’s spyware. We also uncover Discover-Tech, and show how the company helps mercenary surveillance vendors track and hack devices around the world.

October 15, 2026

Bill Marczak, Wolfie Christl, John Scott-Railton, Astrid Perry, Siena Anstis, and Ron Deibert

This report is co-timed with an investigation by Confiant.

This section provides an overview of the online advertising ecosystem, and summarizes our findings about Discover-Tech.

When a user sees an ad on an app or a website, it is likely the result of a real-time auction, where advertisers bid on the chance to show that specific user that specific ad. So-called Real-Time Bidding (RTB) auctions, which are hosted on ad exchanges operated by companies including Google, take place hundreds of billions of times a day. In less than a second, the user’s device initiates a bid request, advertisers submit their bids, and the ad exchange determines the winner of the auction and pushes the ad to the user. Besides an image or video, an online ad can also contain code that runs within the app or browser that shows the ad.

Both advertisers and publishers of apps and websites use ad vendors that act as their intermediaries in these auctions. Advertisers typically buy ads via a so-called Demand-Side Platform (DSP), and a Supply-Side Platform (SSP) sells ad inventory on websites and apps.

Malicious actors make use of two interrelated facets of the online advertising ecosystem:

The advertising ecosystem collects a lot of data and enables individual-level targeting: When a publisher of an app or website wishes to show ads, they add code from an SSP to their app or site. This code collects and shares granular information about the user and their device with ad exchanges to solicit bids for the ad slots. This information can include device identifiers and characteristics, precise location, and IP address data, as well as data about the app or website, and specifications about the ad slot. The DSP or advertiser then examines this information and decides whether they wish to bid on the impression in order to show an ad. The auction system is designed to enable targeting single individuals based on their mobile advertising ID, cookie ID, IP address, and other identifiers.

The advertising ecosystem allows many different third parties to run code in apps and websites: It is tempting to think of an online ad as, simply, a video or image. However, ads themselves may contain code from the advertiser, DSP, and other parties, and run it in the app or browser while the ad is shown to the user, for example to track users, ad impressions, and clicks. Code run by advertisers, DSPs, SSPs, and other third parties within apps and websites is often referred to as “tags”, “pixels”, “SDKs”, or “third-party tracking” more generally.

The totality of information gleaned from ad auctions is quite valuable. A company with access to auction data can track users without their knowledge as they move around in physical space, or switch between cellular, Wi-Fi, and VPNs, by observing how bid requests tied to a specific identifier change location or IP address over time. In fact, the surveillance industry sells access to so-called ad intelligence (ADINT) platforms that leverage this sort of data, often combined with third-party tracking data. In recent years, several investigations and media reports have uncovered vendors that sell ADINT to defense, intelligence, and law enforcement agencies.

Beyond passive data harvesting, malicious parties can also exploit this infrastructure to target certain individuals based on user data included in ad auctions and then run malicious code on their devices. Advertisers or DSPs may run HTML and JavaScript code when an ad is shown to the user. That code retrieves additional JavaScript code, which may, in turn, load further code, such as a browser exploit to install spyware. Since the code can contain identifiers for the user or their device, arbitrary JavaScript code can be sent precisely to a single user’s device. Our research in this report indicates that this architecture is indeed abused to facilitate the delivery of zero-click targeted spyware, and that the simple display of a targeted ad is enough for infection.

There has been some reporting about the intersection between spyware and the advertising ecosystem. However, the specific ways mercenary spyware companies plug into the ads ecosystem to target particular users have remained largely secret. This report exposes zero-click spyware delivered via targeted ads, which we call AdFection, and is the first technical demonstration that mercenary spyware is being distributed via targeted advertisements.

We present technical evidence that the Israel-based company Discover-Tech, while purporting to be a legitimate advertising company, appears to be a front for large-scale ad espionage abuse, including the automatic delivery of mercenary spyware when ads are displayed to a target and the mass profiling and deanonymization of users.

The company serves as a bridge between ad vendors and the mercenary spyware ecosystem. In fact, it appears that serving as this bridge is Discover-Tech’s primary purpose. Its platform, Controlium, allows malicious actors to precisely profile and de-anonymize millions of individuals, fingerprint their devices, and target them with a form of zero-click hacking, where their devices can be automatically infected when an ad is displayed to them.

Discover-Tech appears to work with multiple mercenary spyware, hacking, and advertising vendors, connecting the spyware industry to the online advertising ecosystem. As we detail in this report, Discover-Tech ads are used to infect and profile on behalf of mercenary spyware vendor Candiru. We also detail connections between Discover-Tech and another mercenary hacking company, Bindecy, as well as connections with Intelos, a mercenary ADINT firm.

Discover-Tech is led by its CEO Dekel Boni, who has a background in digital advertising. Eric Banoun, whom Haaretz describes as “one of the pioneers of offensive cyber in Israel”, joined the company’s board of directors soon after it was founded in 2020 and remained there until 2025. Between 2020 and March 2026, Discover-Tech’s shareholders included a company linked to Sara Hamou, who has managed the corporate network of the spyware group Intellexa.

Discover-Tech appears to place advertisements using several techniques. Firstly, the company operates a platform called MyDSP, which interfaces with online ad vendors including Google, Yandex, Vungle (Liftoff), and Sunteng. Secondly, separately from MyDSP, it purchases ads via the ad vendors Eskimi and Comcast-owned Beeswax (Freewheel).

A large number of ads placed by Discover-Tech contain a script tag pointing back to what the company refers to as a “NOAS server” (also called a “getAd server”). This tag causes the ad, when rendered, to connect back to Discover-Tech, submit advertising identifiers for the user (either a cookie ID or a mobile ad ID), and automatically execute any JavaScript code returned. The NOAS server decides, apparently based on a combination of the source IP address and the advertising identifiers, whether the target is eligible to receive any JavaScript. If so, then code is returned. If not, a 0-byte response is returned. The NOAS server is a key part of Discover-Tech’s strategy, allowing Discover-Tech to avoid directly sharing malicious code, or even pointers to malicious code, with the companies who serve and display the ads.

As detailed in Section 9, Discover-Tech appeared on several lists of “certified” and “approved” ad vendors maintained by Google and the advertising industry association IAB Europe from the year 2020 until 2026. These listings helped make Discover-Tech appear to be a legitimate ad vendor and facilitate its participation in the digital advertising ecosystem at scale.

As a result of this investigation, both Google and IAB Europe removed Discover-Tech from their ad vendor registries in early October 2026. Google, which collaborated in the investigation, terminated Discover-Tech’s access to its ad exchange platforms.  Beeswax removed Discover-Tech from its ad buying platform, Vungle (Liftoff) paused Discover-Tech’s access while conducting a review, and Eskimi blocked Discover-Tech’s accounts and domains.

In this report we provide an overview of the different types of ad abuse facilitated by Discover-Tech, the company’s ad targeting systems and practices, as well as its partners and corporate network.

In Section 2, we show how Candiru works with Discover-Tech to conduct AdFection attacks, and describe one such attack: the targeting and infection of devices at the international media network Al Jazeera with Candiru’s mercenary spyware.

In Section 3, we examine Controlium, a Discover-Tech platform that provides a control-panel style interface enabling mercenary spyware customers to target specific users with “controlled ads.”

In Section 4, we examine links between Discover-Tech and mercenary spyware companies Candiru/Integrity Labs and Bindecy. We then outline their relationships with other mercenary surveillance companies, including advertising intelligence (ADINT) vendor Intelos, and an ADINT vendor we refer to as DARK CARTOGRAPHER, which is building databases linking users’ mobile advertising identifiers to their phone numbers.

In Section 5, we analyze where Discover-Tech’s malicious advertisements land. We identified a Discover-Tech server that published almost four billion ad bidding records. These records show that Discover-Tech ads were served in almost 200,000 different Android apps, iOS apps, and websites in many countries. We also highlight specific countries and government networks where Discover-Tech’s advertisements had impressions.

In Section 6, we use technical analysis to examine how Discover-Tech deploys ads, tracks users and exchanges user identifiers with other ad vendors, including with Beeswax, Yandex, and Microsoft’s ad system Xandr.

In Section 7, we present our research on Discover-Tech Ltd, its corporate network, key persons linked to the company, the origins of its MyDSP advertising technology, and its connection to the wider advertising ecosystem.

In Section 8, we summarize what is known about the mercenary surveillance firms Candiru, Bindecy, and Intelos, and we further examine their activities and corporate networks in the context of the findings presented in our report.

In Section 9, we explore how major industry organizations and ad vendors helped enable Discover-Tech’s ad operations, including Google, IAB Europe, Beeswax (FreeWheel/Comcast), Vungle (Liftoff), Eskimi, Sunteng, and Xandr (Microsoft).

In Section 10, we discuss the implications of AdFection for user security and human rights.

In Section 11, we provide recommendations to lawmakers, regulators, defenders, and the advertising industry on how to mitigate and block threats from AdFection-style attacks.

The Citizen Lab sent requests for comment to 13 companies; their responses are included in full in the ‘Correspondence with Companies’ section.

This section provides the first public technical confirmation of a zero-click spyware attack via targeted ads in the wild: the targeting and infection of devices at the international media network Al Jazeera with mercenary spyware. We refer to this type of attack as AdFection. Using network analysis, infrastructure fingerprinting, and analysis of implant behaviour, we connect Discover-Tech’s infrastructure with the distribution of Candiru’s mercenary spyware.

The instances of Candiru AdFection via Discover-Tech ads all share similar characteristics. First, Discover-Tech wins a bid, and one of their ads is pushed to a website or app that is open on a user’s device. The user may see this ad, such as in Figure 4, though in some cases the ad may render in the background.

When the website or app receives the ad, it renders it, requesting JavaScript from a Discover-Tech server embedded within the ad. In most cases, the user who sees the ad is not selected for targeting, and the server will not return any JavaScript to be executed.  Nevertheless, the ad will still gather data from the user’s browser and submit it back to Discover-Tech, which can include cookies set on the webpage including the ad, as well as the device’s public IPv6 address.

In 2024 and 2025, international news network Al Jazeera was targeted in a series of zero-click attacks that we link with high confidence to Candiru’s spyware delivered via Discover-Tech’s ads. At least 45 devices within Al Jazeera were targeted in these attacks.

Analysis of network logs provided to the Citizen Lab by Al Jazeera collected during the attack period provides a clear temporal signature of how the attack was executed. Infected devices first show contact with domains from Discover-Tech infrastructure, indicating an ad impression. Next, the devices show connections with a Candiru validator server. The validator server performs an initial check of the device before it is further profiled and infected. Ultimately, an infected device communicates with a Candiru Command and Control (C&C) server. This temporal signature is illustrated by Figure 5.

We developed a fingerprint for Candiru validator servers. Both keyadapter[.]com and sharethere[.]net returned banners that matched the following regular expression on Censys.1  We refer to this as Fingerprint V1:

We found hosts on Censys matching Fingerprint V1 between August 2022 through July 2026, though we note that in May and June 2026, this behaviour gradually began being retired. In all, we found 305 distinct domain names on 319 IP addresses, though to save query costs we only searched one historical Censys snapshot per month. The set of 305 validator server domains we found includes ones publicly attributed to Candiru by Sekoia, as well as Recorded Future.

We also identified a separate fingerprint for the C&C servers used in the attack, Fingerprint C1. Four of the servers matched it (fearevolve[.]com, insightenterprisells[.]com, jobmarcher[.]com, plasticbells[.]com). We could not locate a response in Internet scanning data for the other three.

Al Jazeera isolated a Windows DLL file from one of the compromised devices which contains hardcoded Command & Control servers matching Fingerprint C1. The sample is available on VirusTotal.

Candiru spyware sample SHA256: 255869de85e2a171993fc5eb8a556d873a1b8966e040f6f55926f2fa2d595cc8

This sample hard-codes two C&C servers that match Fingerprint C1: fearevolve[.]com and jobmarcher[.]com. The functionality broadly overlaps with the functionality of the Candiru chain from our 2021 report. For example:

The combination of the COM persistence hijack, the use of a distinctive 48-byte repeating XOR obfuscation technique with a “dummy” null terminator, and the specific hardcoded network connectivity check leads us to conclude with high confidence that this sample is a newer version of the Candiru attack chain that we captured in 2021.

This section examines Controlium, a platform that provides a control-panel style interface allowing mercenary spyware customers to target specific users with “controlled ads” that deliver malware. Discover-Tech published the full source code for Controlium’s frontend on the app’s login page, which allowed us to review and reconstruct the user interface.

Discover-Tech provides its customers with access to a platform called Controlium that appears to be specifically designed to allow them to push malicious content to individual targeted users alongside advertisements. Customers can use Controlium to select a user for infection or profiling based on their mobile advertising identifier (iOS or Android), browser identifier (MyDSP or Beeswax cookie ID), and/or IP address. Discover-Tech’s malicious ads (referred to as “controlled ads”) sometimes also contain branding of companies that are closely linked to Discover-Tech, or branding from apparently unwitting third-party companies, including Amazon and AliExpress. We have no evidence that these ads were purchased by Amazon or AliExpress.

As is standard for many web apps, the entirety of the source code for the Controlium frontend is included on the app’s login page. We visited the login page in a web browser and saved the page to disk to obtain a copy of the frontend.2 We modified our copy of the code to remove any communication with any external servers, and to reveal all available screens in the UI. We then opened this version in a web browser to explore the app’s user interface.

In our analysis of Controlium, we downloaded only publicly accessible resources without circumventing any access controls. Most data associated with Controlium, such as information about Discover-Tech’s customers and their operations, is intentionally protected with an authorization token. However, we were able to obtain data on Controlium user logins from an unauthenticated API endpoint (see below: ‘Unauthenticated Endpoint’). We also assess that it would have been possible for a hacker to spoof a valid authorization (see below: ‘Authentication Vulnerability’), although we did not test this.

We found the Controlium platform available on the following websites:

These domain names all had CNAME records pointing to an AWS Application Load Balancer (ALB) with the name:

Additionally, several strings in the Controlium code directly reference Discover-Tech:

Furthermore, if a user tries to access a particular endpoint in the app called “/jsConfig”, the app displays the following message, which is a possible reference to Discover-Tech’s CEO Dekel Boni:

Finally, an unauthenticated API endpoint (see below: ‘Unauthenticated Endpoint’) shows frequent login activity from users whose names overlap with Discover-Tech employees on LinkedIn.

An account designated as an “admin” on the Controlium platform can configure a number of different parameters for customers of the platform. First, an admin may grant a customer access to the web interface, or the API. It also appears that the Controlium product can be “white labeled” with a different logo, and that access can be restricted to specific IPs.

Next, admins may add restrictions on what type of campaigns a customer may run. These restrictions control which combinations of user IDs and IP addresses they are allowed to bid on, and which “URL Types” they can access.

Customers can have certain “OpSec” restrictions placed on their ad bidding, which appears to be an effort to ensure that customers are not bidding too frequently or too broadly:

There is also another type of “OpSec” called “Ad URL OpSec”, which we explore more in Section 4.

Customers can be further restricted based on how many campaigns they can run daily or monthly, or restricted based on a “Domains Whitelist” or “Apps Whitelist”, which appear to control on which domain or within which mobile apps ads can be bid on. As is customary for licensing of an attack platform, customers can be restricted to only bid on ads in certain countries via either an allowlist or blocklist.

The exact steps a user or customer would need to take to use the platform are not clear. The Controlium user interface includes a number of modules and forms that provide, in part, overlapping functionality to set up ad campaigns and monitor ad data.

Controlium users can create a “tag”, which defines a combination of an ad image, a landing page, a “NOAS URL” (see below: ‘A Look at the NOAS Server’), and URLs for logging impressions and clicks.

Users can select a DSP to use for delivering the ad. The available options include Beeswax, Eskimi and Discover-Tech’s own MyDSP. When selecting MyDSP, they can also choose whether to use the Google or Yandex ad exchange.

Controlium’s “OP Creative Upload” module allows users to upload and configure advertising content (e.g. an ad), and then upload the data to a DSP. Users can attach a tag to the ad either by defining a landing page, a NOAS URL and URLs for logging impressions and clicks, or they can paste a “Custom Tag” generated by the “Tag Generation” module.

The available DSP options include “MyDSP WW”, “MyDSP Yandex RU”, “Beeswax (Palm 3)”, “MyDSP Google (Palm 3)”, and others. Users can also select several “Add Ons” including “Infinite FIFO”, “Detect Zuid”, and “User Agent”.

Another module labeled “Campaigns” allows Controlium users to associate “Ad URLs” to selected “controlled ads”, which can be served either in mobile apps or on websites, according to Controlium’s source code. As shown in the screenshot, the module allows users to define target “User IDs” and select a “URL Type”.

The URL types available for selection include “Ad URL”, “Test URL”, “Script”, “User Agent”, “Monitor”, “Pixel”, and “De-anon”. We are unsure what most of these options mean, but we think that for “Ad URL”, the NOAS server returns JavaScript adding a 1×1 iframe to the page pointing at the specified URL, and “Script” may be designed to allow arbitrary JavaScript to run. Any URL is delivered via the NOAS Server (see below: ‘A Look at the NOAS Server’).

While the data associated with Controlium’s customers and their operations are nominally protected with an authorization token, it appears that it would be easy for a hacker to spoof a valid token. We did not attempt to exploit this issue, as we believe doing so would have constituted unauthorized access to Discover-Tech’s systems.

The underlying issue stems from Discover-Tech’s improper use of Okta’s Auth0 product. When a Controlium customer authenticates with Auth0, a JWT is returned to their browser. This token is digitally signed by Auth0, and contains information about scopes and expiry that the backend server should validate. However, Controlium ignores this token and instead passes a separate user object as a token to the backend server. The user object simply contains unauthenticated metadata about the user, such as their name and email address. Controlium encrypts this information with a secret key published in the Controlium platform.

Interestingly, the correct code to use the JWT as an authorization token was present within the Controlium platform, but was commented out in lieu of the vulnerable code.

During our analysis of the Controlium platform, we observed that the source code mentioned an endpoint called “/csv-download”, which accepted start and end date parameters.  When we sent normal HTTP GET requests to this endpoint without any password, special headers, or authentication token, we received logs showing which users had logged in to Controlium, and from which IP addresses.  We successfully exported authentication logs for 128 days and identified 120 distinct usernames logging into the Controlium instances on controlium[.]net and powerium[.]net. We further delve into this data in Section 4.

We were able to elicit code from NOAS servers by testing “dummy” User ID values. For example, we observed that a visit to:

Yielded the following content:

We also found that we could task a NOAS server for a similar Discover-Tech app published on events-ui.myweb3id[.]io called “Mini Platform C”.

We input a User ID, “test123” into this form, and an AD URL, “https://example.com/”, then we observed the tasking by visiting this NOAS URL:

The first time we visited it, the URL returned this:

Subsequent visits returned nothing.

This version of “Mini Platform C” does not appear to support any other options besides “Ad URL” for tasking the NOAS server. A similar version of the “Mini Platform C” app is also available on the site events-ui.discover-tech[.]io. The JavaScript code for both app versions is available on archive.org (1, 2).

The Controlium platform provides several additional modules, according to our analysis of the app’s user interface and source code.

Two Controlium modules named “Targeting” (also known as “Targeting Config”) and “cTargeting” (also known as “Upload Audiences”) allow users to upload digital identifiers referring to single or multiple targets, including mobile advertising IDs for Android and Apple devices, Beeswax user IDs, MyDSP user IDs and IP addresses. The “Targeting Config” module attaches the uploaded identifiers to a “segment”, a widely used term that describes lists of identifiers to be used for targeting in digital advertising.

Controlium users can view data on ad impressions for a target identifier or IP address in the last 30 minutes:

A similar module named “Bid Requests” allows users to view data on recent ad bid requests for a specific target identifier or IP address. It provides a list of records that contain user IDs, the website visited or app used by the user, the IP address of the user’s device and other attributes.

The “Events Logger” module provides access to activity records related to ad serving. The available data sources in another Controlium module named “OP Reporting” include MyDSP, Beeswax, Google, and Facebook. We are unsure what kind of reporting data would be displayed by that module. The “Ads Dashboard” module provides reports about ad impressions, the number of users reached and the amount spent (in $) for active campaigns.

Three Controlium modules named “User Info”, “User API Info”, and “User Sync Info” appear to provide key/value information on specific users upon entering user identifiers. They mention a number of attributes which we do not fully understand. For example, they offer to display user identifiers labeled “UUED” and “UUPD”. One module provides a “User ID Type” selection. The available options include “EYield”, “TYield”, “VYield”, “SYield”, “Sync_User”, “Sync_Domain”, “Sync_App”, “AH_User”. Some of these options appear to be related to user ID syncing across different vendors, which is further examined in Section 6.

The modules that provide access to information on bid requests, ad impressions, events, and users can be used for troubleshooting and verification purposes, but also to spy on targets and other users whose data is in the bid requests.

This section examines links between Discover-Tech and the mercenary spyware companies Candiru and Bindecy. We also illustrate that, beyond facilitating mercenary spyware delivery, Discover-Tech is linked to ADINT firms, including Intelos. Discover-Tech also supports mass-deanonymization of internet and app users by a threat actor we call DARK CARTOGRAPHER, which exploits vulnerabilities in mobile networks to unmask users’ phone numbers.

We observed that Discover-Tech sends encrypted ad impression data to Candiru using Controlium’s “Ad URL OpSec” feature. We identified several 2024 and 2025 Candiru infection links to at least six domains matching Fingerprint V1 and that also contained a parameter “?q=” whose value was 16 bytes of data in Base64-encoded form. In every case, the value of the “?q=” parameter was correctly decrypted with the “V1” AES-256 key published on a page called “Ad URL OpSec Decoder” on the website myipinfo[.]io. The website myipinfo[.]io is clearly linked to Discover-Tech: passive DNS data shows multiple overlaps in IP addresses and CNAME records with other Discover-Tech websites, including powerium[.]net and myweb3id[.]io (see also Section 7).

One case of a Candiru infection link bearing a Discover-Tech Ad URL OpSec parameter is listed publicly on VirusTotal. The “?q=” parameter decrypts to an IP registered at the Saudi Ministry of Foreign Affairs, indicating that organization as a potential target of Candiru spyware via Discover-Tech ads:

We assess that this opsec data is included to facilitate a secure handoff from Discover-Tech to an attacker. The attacker presumably compares the visitor IP for the infection link against the IP encrypted by Discover-Tech, to make sure the link from the ad impression was not silently swapped to a different device (as a security researcher might want to do to capture an exploit).

Based on our analysis of Controlium user logins from an unauthenticated API endpoint (Section 3), we identified two users who logged in to Controlium from an IP address in Israel that we attribute to Candiru/Integrity Labs. One of these users, which we refer to as INTEGRITYPRESALE1, matched the name of someone listed on LinkedIn as having a “Head of Presale” position in Israel at “Cyber Security Company”. The “Cyber Security Company” page is nominally for a Jakarta-based company, but we think the user selected this page because it has a generic name that conveys the industry in which they work without naming the specific company. Viewing the “Cyber Security Company” page on LinkedIn shows “Integrity Labs”, “NSO Group”, and “Integrity Lab” (apparently a typo of “Integrity Labs”) in the top three spots in the “pages people also viewed” panel.

The second user signing in from the Integrity Labs IP address, which we refer to as INTEGRITYPRESALE2, has a username that appears to include a first name, and ends in “_pap_pres”.  We suspect the “_pres” stands for “presale”.  There is a user on LinkedIn who shares a first name with this user, and is a “Presales Engineer” at “Cyber Security Company”, though we cannot be certain it is the same individual.

We identified INTEGRITYPRESALE1 and 2 signing into Controlium from locations in the following countries: Azerbaijan, Czechia, Israel, Italy, Mexico, Montenegro, UAE, and the United States.

We are unsure what the phrase “pap” refers to, but we noted only two other usernames that contained the string “pap”. They were part of a cluster of users signing in exclusively from the local IP address 10.0.0.52, suggesting these as further possible Candiru-linked users:

We identified Discover-Tech ads that sought to exploit the well-known “WebRTC IP Leak” issue, which can potentially reveal the IP address of VPN and proxy users. The same ads also attempted to unmask the phone number (MSISDN) of mobile users who were served the impression. The MSISDN leaks exploit various issues, including widespread problems with so-called “zero-click login” technologies, which aim to facilitate frictionless authentication and purchases for users on their mobile devices.

One way “zero-click login” operates is that mobile providers select certain websites for “HTTP header enrichment,” so that when plaintext HTTP requests pass through the provider’s mobile gateway, an HTTP header (like X-MSISDN) is added to the request that provides the user’s phone number to the website. As an alternative to HTTP header enrichment, third-party services may work directly with the telco to facilitate this “zero-click login”. There appear to be widespread bugs with this allowlist matching, as well as bugs or security issues in third-party enrichment providers. While mainstream web browsers such as Chrome are moving towards blocking any non-HTTPS requests, it is likely that the app ecosystem will still embed webviews that permit non-HTTPS content.

We taxonomized the issues into five types, exploited by attackers across numerous mobile providers in more than 30 countries in North America, South America, Europe, Africa, and Asia, and disclosure to companies is in progress. Once the disclosure process is complete, we will release our subsequent report delving into technical analysis and attribution of these attacks.

It is rare to see such direct overlaps between mercenary vendors and U.S. government or intelligence contractors. In this section we show how, beyond targeting users of mobile apps, Discover-Tech deploys a range of techniques to deliver ads and track users while they browse across websites. This involves Discover-Tech running its own code in the user’s web browser, both while deploying ads to users and independently of showing them ads. We explore Discover-Tech’s “Banner Tester” tool to show how the company generates tracking tags and pixels attached to ads, including code that connects to a NOAS server, which we identified as a vector for spyware delivery. We also document how Discover-Tech engages in “ID syncing” with other ad vendors, and how it leverages IAB Europe’s “Transparency and Consent Framework” to appear GDPR-compliant, even while facilitating unwanted and malicious activity.

An ad displayed to a website visitor consists of an image or video to be shown and a link to be clicked, but can also carry HTML and JavaScript code that connects to one or more domains in order to track users, ad impressions, clicks, and other activities. This code is typically referred to as an ad tag. A related concept, a so-called tracking pixel, also describes code running in the web browser that connects to third-party ad vendors. Ad vendors use additional tracking code for user ID syncing by exchanging user identifiers with each other in order to identify, profile, and target website visitors across sites and vendors.

Our analysis of ad tags, tracking pixels, and ID syncing activities associated with Discover-Tech’s ad delivery is based on an analysis of publicly available code, browser testing and ad transactions archived by the web investigation tool urlscan. While ads displayed in mobile apps similarly carry code that connects to ad vendors, this section focuses on Discover-Tech ads displayed in the web browser.

Unlike apps on mobile devices, web browsers do not allow websites to access a universal device identifier. The process of “ID syncing”, often also referred to as “cookie syncing”, addresses this lack of a universal user identifier. Research shows that digital advertising firms and data brokers use sophisticated forms of ID syncing to identify, profile and target web users across vendors. They achieve this by constantly exchanging user identifiers with each other, storing them in the browser and retrieving them again while users visit different websites that embed third-party tracking code.

We found evidence showing how Discover-Tech engages in ID syncing with Comcast’s ad system Beeswax, Yandex, and Microsoft’s ad platform Xandr.

Discover-Tech appears to use its myweb3id[.]io domain for ID syncing with Yandex. This domain is highly prevalent as a tracking domain on a large number of websites. Starting in May 2025, urlscan archived more than 10,000 records that include third-party requests to the domain events.myweb3id[.]io, most of them occurring during visits to Russian websites.

Discover-Tech appears to use another domain, tracookiepixel[.]xyz, which is associated with myweb3id[.]io via DNS links and which is also highly prevalent as a tracking domain on a large number of websites, for ID syncing with Beeswax. Starting in July 2025, urlscan archived more than 10,000 records that include third-party requests to tracookiepixel[.]xyz, many of them occurring during visits to popular websites including IMDb and New York Times.

A recent urlscan record shows an example request chain that was initiated during a visit to the website of The Guardian, which involves ID syncing across Discover-Tech’s tracookiepixel[.]xyz domain and Beeswax’ tracking domain bidr[.]io. The requests contain the parameter “bee_sync_partners=dtech”, which indicates some kind of business relationship between Discover-Tech and Beeswax.

These ID syncing activities typically take place during website visits even when a user was not served a Discover-Tech ad. We are unsure how exactly Discover-Tech uses its browser ID syncing capabilities. Generally, being able to synchronize and correlate user identities across vendors is considered a precondition for individual-level ad targeting in the web browser. The Controlium platform, as examined in Section 3, offers to upload lists of Beeswax identifiers for ad targeting in its “cTargeting” module, among mobile advertising IDs, IP addresses, and other identifiers, based on our analysis of the source code.

We conclude that many websites make constant requests to Discover-Tech’s domains events.myweb3id[.]io and tracookiepixel[.]xyz in the background. These requests serve the purpose of ID syncing with Beeswax and Yandex, and Discover-Tech’s domains receive, in addition to user identifiers, at least the website visitor’s IP address and information about their browser and operating system.

Once loaded on a website, the code stores user identifiers associated with Discover-Tech, Beeswax, and Xandr in the user’s web browser in order to retrieve them again during subsequent visits to websites that load the same code.

The code is designed to initiate the ID syncing process by sending Discover-Tech’s user identifier to Beeswax and Yandex in order to receive corresponding Beeswax and Yandex identifiers. Discover-Tech has been deeply embedded and interconnected with the digital advertising industry for years. In this section, we further investigate Discover-Tech, key persons affiliated with the company, related companies, and the origins of its MyDSP advertising technology.

Discover-Tech purports to be a typical digital advertising firm, offering a so-called Demand-Side Platform (DSP), which facilitates the delivery of targeted ads. On its website, it claims to have “unrestricted access to top-ranking apps with 1+ billion daily active users” via a “worldwide ad exchange”. In addition to its DSP, Discover-Tech offers “monetization” solutions to mobile network operators and mobile device manufacturers, which we discuss further below.

Israeli company records we reviewed link Discover-Tech’s website, discover-tech[.]io, to the company Discover-Tech Ltd registered in March 2020, with Dekel Boni listed as its initial director and sole shareholder. In the two months after its incorporation, Eric Banoun, who is a major figure in the Israeli surveillance technology industry, joined Discover-Tech’s board of directors, and the shareholder base was expanded. From April 2020, the company’s shareholders included Dekel Boni, Guy Lants, Yaniv Basil, Zfanya Leib, Sergei Bartashevich, and Chaia Services Ltd, a company registered in the British Virgin Islands. Eric Banoun left the company’s board of directors in January 2025 and Chaia Services Ltd ceased to be a shareholder in March 2026. As of July 2026, Discover-Tech is directed by Dekel Boni and owned by Boni, Basil, and Lants.

Eric Banoun co-founded the cyberespionage firm Circles, a close NSO Group affiliate, and Senpai Technologies, which is part of the Intellexa consortium. We could not access corporate registration information on Discover-Tech’s shareholder Chaia Services Ltd. However, a Haaretz investigation reported that one of Chaia’s directors was Sara Hamou. Hamou managed Intellexa’s corporate network and was sentenced to eight years in prison (pending appeal) by a Greek court for her role in the Predatorgate scandal. Eric Banoun was listed as a director of a similarly named U.S.-based company, Chaia Services Tech LLC, which was dissolved in 2025.

Based on the links to Eric Banoun and Chaia Services Ltd., we conclude that Discover-Tech was linked to the spyware industry for almost six years, according to Israeli company records and other publicly available information.

Discover-Tech’s other shareholders, including Dekel Boni who is now the company’s sole director, have a background in digital advertising, previously working for adtech firms like Digital Turbine and Taptica, according to their LinkedIn profiles.3 Boni lists himself as Discover-Tech’s CEO, Guy Lants as its “Director of Product”. Yaniv Basil lists himself as the company’s “Chief Technology Officer” between 2020 and 2023.

Despite information about Discover-Tech’s links to figures in the spyware industry that could be readily obtained from a review of corporate records, major advertising industry organizations added the company to several lists of “certified” or “approved” ad vendors, which helped make the company appear to be a legitimate advertising firm and facilitated its participation in the advertising ecosystem at scale.

As discussed in Section 9, Google listed Discover-Tech among its “Ad Manager Certified External Vendors”, “Ad Technology Partners”, and “Ads Personalization Providers” from 2020 until 2026. The advertising industry association IAB Europe listed the company on the “Global Vendor List” for its “Transparency & Consent Framework” (TCF), also from 2020 until 2026. In Section 9, we examine the implications of Discover-Tech’s ad vendor registrations with Google and IAB Europe in detail.

Both the Google and IAB vendor registrations consistently refer to the Israeli company Discover-Tech Ltd and the domain discover-tech[.]io. In addition, Google’s list of “Ads Personalization providers” clearly links Discover-Tech to the domains  mtrtb[.]com and mydsp[.]io, which it listed among “domains which can be attributed to the provider” Discover-Tech Ltd.

According to historical whois information, Discover-Tech Ltd took ownership of both domains in 2020. Both mtrtb[.]com and mydsp[.]io can be “attributed” to Discover-Tech Ltd according to Google, as discussed in Section 9.

The current discover-tech.io site promises to help mobile network operators and mobile device manufacturers benefit from “sponsored and tailored app recommendations”, in addition to the company’s DSP offering. In 2021, Discover-Tech Ltd operated a mobile app on behalf of the Serbian subsidiary of the mobile network operator A1 Telekom Austria, according to a terms of use agreement, which explains that the app would provide A1 customers with content from both A1 and Discover-Tech. The description on the 2021 version of the Serbian A1 website suggests that the app, named “Moy A1” (“My A1”), enabled A1 customers to check their mobile plan, download invoices, and buy additional credits. The 2020 version of the Discover-Tech lists A1 and device manufacturers like Samsung, Tecno, and Wiko among the company’s customers. We did not further investigate Discover-Tech’s mobile carrier and device manufacturer business, which may or may not be active anymore.

In conclusion, we believe that Discover-Tech emerged from both RelevanTech and MyDSP, both previously owned by Glispa. While MyDSP and additional software for the delivery of malicious ads appear to be operational in 2026, an asset sale discussed in the next subsection suggests that Discover-Tech may not offer its services for mobile carriers and device manufacturers anymore.

In 2021, the Dubai-based firm Affle MEA FZ-LLC, part of the mobile advertising group Affle, based in Singapore and India, acquired “business assets” from Discover-Tech Ltd, according to public filings. Publicly available financial statements refer to the acquisition of a Discover-Tech “business segment” including “brand, IP, domain, business relationships and goodwill”.

An Affle press release quotes Discover-Tech founder Dekel Boni stating that he was “proud” that Discover-Tech’s “technology” that “powers the first interaction a user has with his new device” would become part of the “app discover offering” of Appnext, another company acquired by Affle.

Based on the information available to us, we believe that Discover-Tech Ltd sold its offerings for mobile carriers and device vendors examined in the previous subsection, to Affle. We have no reason to believe that Affle has any control over Discover-Tech’s malicious ad operations that we investigate in this report. However, the exact scope of this asset sale remains unknown to us. Affle did not respond to our request for comment within the timeline provided.

Candiru is an Israeli-founded mercenary spyware company that draws its original name from the parasitic Candiru fish, and has operated under a wide range of names throughout the years, including Saito Tech. Today, Candiru operates under the rebranded identity of Integrity Labs after acquisition by U.S.-based Integrity Partners.

Candiru is a mercenary spyware threat actor known by multiple names, including SOURGUM and Carmel Tsunami by Microsoft.

First Candiru Abuse Discoveries: 2021

On July 15, 2021, the Citizen Lab published the first report exposing Candiru. That investigation included identifying a Candiru victim and recovering a copy of Candiru’s Windows spyware. We then worked with Microsoft’s Threat Intelligence Center (MSTIC) to analyze the spyware, which led to the identification of two zero-day vulnerabilities (CVE-2021-31979 and CVE-2021-33771). We also identified over 750 websites linked to Candiru’s infection infrastructure that masqueraded as a wide range of civil society entities ranging from media organizations to Amnesty International.

On July 14, 2021, Google TAG published a report which included discussion of two Chrome exploits (CVE-2021-21166 and CVE-2021-30551) that pointed to addresses matching our Candiru fingerprint. The report also linked a Microsoft Office exploit (CVE-2021-33742) to the same operator.

Microsoft’s own investigation into Candiru, published simultaneously with our report on July 15, 2021, identified at least 100 spyware victims across ten countries. Microsoft reported that the victims included journalists, opposition politicians, dissidents, and activists.

On November 16, 2021, ESET reported on a series of watering hole attacks observed in 2020 and 2021 targeting websites in the Middle East with what they described as a “strong focus on Yemen.” They attributed the attacks to Candiru.

Further Investigations and Abuses: 2022-2025

In 2022, the Citizen Lab again found Candiru spyware targeting victims among Catalan civil society groups in Spain. In that investigation, we identified signs of a live Candiru infection on a Catalan university network, and successfully worked with system administrators to identify the victim, isolate the device, and extract the active spyware. The targeting we observed as part of this campaign included emails masquerading as official Spanish governmental messages about COVID.

On July 21, 2022, Avast published a report revealing that Candiru was using a Chrome zero-day exploiting WebRTC (CVE-2022-2294), and found evidence of targeting of users in multiple countries in the Middle East.

On December 22, 2022, Meta disclosed that it disrupted around 130 Facebook and Instagram accounts used by Candiru to send infection links amongst themselves to “test phishing capabilities.”

In the summer of 2024, during the parliamentary election campaign, Member of the European Parliament (MEP) Daniel Freund was targeted with Candiru’s mercenary spyware, according to the European Parliament’s security services.

On August 5, 2025, Recorded Future’s Insikt Group investigated Candiru infrastructure and identified multiple Candiru clusters linked to Hungary, Saudi Arabia, Indonesia, and Azerbaijan, among others.

On September 2, 2025, Sekoia published an investigation into Candiru’s spyware, highlighting how Candiru and similar companies leverage complex jurisdictional structures to avoid discovery.

On November 3, 2021, Candiru was added to the United States Commerce Department’s Entity List for malicious cyber activities. The entity listing noted that Candiru was added because “they developed and supplied spyware to foreign governments that used this tool to maliciously target government officials, journalists, businesspeople, activists, academics, and embassy workers.”

In October 2024, Daniel Freund filed a criminal complaint with the assistance of German digital rights NGO GFF against Viktor Orbán and unnamed persons over his targeting with Candiru.

On April 30, 2025, the NGO Sentinel Alliance filed a case against multiple Spanish governmental entities, NSO Group, and Candiru over the mercenary spyware attacks targeting Catalan civil society.

In April 2025, Israeli media reported that U.S.-based Integrity Partners acquired the operations of Candiru for $30 million in a bid to bypass the U.S. Entity Listing. Research by Recorded Future’s Insikt Group identified Candiru as having been rebranded to “Integrity Labs”  (אינטגריטי לאבס בע~מ) in December 2024. The current status of the acquisition is unclear.

Candiru/Integrity Labs did not respond to our request for comment within the timeline provided.

This section explores how major industry organizations and ad vendors helped enable Discover-Tech’s ad operations, and notes that Discover-Tech achieved “certified” and “approved” status by Google and the major advertising industry association IAB Europe.

Our analysis indicates that Discover-Tech deployed ads via Google, Yandex, and other ad vendors including Beeswax (FreeWheel/Comcast), Vungle (Liftoff), Eskimi, and Sunteng. In addition, both Google and the advertising association IAB Europe have listed Discover-Tech as a “certified” and “approved” ad vendor since the year 2020, which helped make the company appear to be a legitimate advertising firm and facilitate its participation in the advertising ecosystem at scale.

As a result of this investigation, both Google and IAB Europe removed Discover-Tech from their ad vendor registries in early October 2026. Google, which collaborated in the investigation, terminated Discover-Tech’s access to its ad exchange platforms. Beeswax removed Discover-Tech from its ad buying platform. Vungle (Liftoff) paused Discover-Tech’s access while conducting a review. Eskimi blocked Discover-Tech’s accounts and domains.

The ad vendors identified in this section are distinct from mercenary spyware or ADINT vendors insofar as they are not necessarily aware of potential misuses of their infrastructure for non-advertising purposes.

Google listed Discover-Tech Ltd among its roughly 2,400 Certified External Vendors. Google also listed Discover-Tech among its roughly 1,000 Ad Technology Providers, who can receive data on website visitors and app users in Europe. Discover-Tech Ltd was added to all these lists in 2020. Google, which collaborated in this investigation, removed Discover-Tech from its ad vendor registries and terminated the company’s access to its ad exchange platforms as of the first week of October, 2026.

Discover-Tech Ltd was also listed in the Global Vendor List (GVL) maintained by the European branch of the Interactive Advertising Bureau (IAB), a key digital advertising industry association. The GVL contains roughly 1,000 vendors that are “registered and approved” by IAB Europe. These vendors can participate in IAB Europe’s “Transparency & Consent Framework” (TCF), which promises to enable ad vendors to comply with European data protection and privacy law when processing personal data for digital advertising purposes. While the TCF’s ability to enable lawful data processing is controversially debated, a GVL registration has become a de-facto requirement for an ad vendor to participate in digital advertising, display ads and receive data in Europe. IAB Europe added Discover-Tech Ltd to the GVL on July 2, 2020. As a result of this investigation, Discover-Tech was removed from the GVL on October 8, 2026.

According to IAB Europe, it takes “reasonable steps to vet and approve” vendor applications, including the “identity of the party or parties controlling the vendor” and the vendor’s ability to “adhere” to a number of TCF policies, and then monitors their compliance with those policies. The TCF is the basis for passing user “consent” signals for personal data processing across the digital advertising supply chain, from users to publishers to intermediaries (like SSPs, DSPs, and ad exchanges) to advertisers, including in bid requests and tracking pixels. Most ad tags and tracking pixels that connect to third-party vendors require “consent” signals, including in some jurisdictions outside Europe and the U.K. like California. Google, Xandr, and most larger ad platforms require TCF compliance. While several studies found that vendors are too often ignoring “consent” signals, an ad vendor that is not listed in the GVL, and thus cannot pass any signal, can hardly interface with other ad vendors in reliable ways.

While the vendor lists maintained by Google and the IAB Europe help a company appear to be a legitimate ad vendor and are the basis to participate in the digital advertising ecosystem in a reliable way at scale, they appear to be largely based on self-attestation by vendors. They are also the basis for most of the “consent” popups shown to European web and app users every day. Discover-Tech Ltd’s inclusion in those lists potentially means that, for almost six years, hundreds of millions of Europeans were presented with a consent request that, if the recipient clicked “Agree,” could be construed as authorizing Discover-Tech to process their data under the GDPR.

As of October 2026, Discover-Tech is additionally listed in a registry operated by the “Trustworthy Accountability Group” (TAG) created by major U.S. advertising associations and the IAB, which aims to increase trust in the digital advertising industry, eliminate fraud and fight criminal activity including “malware threats targeting the digital advertising supply chain”. The Verified by TAG badge held by Discover-Tech, which the company also displays on its website, is used across the industry to “determine trust and transparency” and let prospective partners know that a company has taken “actionable steps to verify their identities and adopt rigorous standards to fight online fraud, piracy, malware, and lack of transparency”, according to the TAG website.

Our analysis of ad bidding data in Section 5 indicates that Discover-Tech targeted users by participating in ad auctions handled by Google, Yandex, and other ad vendors including Vungle and Sunteng. The analysis of the Controlium platform in Sections 3 and 6 indicates that Discover-Tech also uses the ad buying platforms Beeswax DSP and Eskimi DSP to target users. In addition, those sections show that Discover-Tech receives and utilizes user identifiers maintained by Microsoft’s advertising platform Xandr.

This report provides the first-ever technical evidence of zero-click mercenary spyware attacks delivered via targeted advertising. We also confirm that AdFection was used to infect devices at international media organization Al Jazeera.

These attacks were facilitated by Discover-Tech, which presents itself as a legitimate advertising business but actually serves as a bridge between mercenary spyware companies and the advertising ecosystem. Discover-Tech not only helps companies like Candiru use ads to mass-profile unwitting phone users, their ads directly enable these companies to silently infect selected targets’ devices.

The combination of advertising intelligence and the delivery of spyware is extremely concerning, for several reasons. First, both the digital advertising and mercenary spyware industry are very poorly regulated, with the latter featuring numerous firms notorious for deception, a lack of transparency, and even unlawful activities. To see entities from those two industries forming an alliance should be a wakeup call to regulators and policymakers around the world. Dozens of reports by numerous organizations, including the Citizen Lab, have shown incontrovertible proof of the harms caused by mercenary spyware vendors on civil society around the globe. With the addition of the type of advertising intelligence capabilities we have documented, those firms’ capabilities will now be supercharged.

Second, the combination of advertising intelligence and spyware infections provide government security agencies with highly invasive systems that span both mass and highly targeted types of user surveillance. As we show in this report, millions of devices were likely unwittingly profiled as a form of preliminary reconnaissance to enable targeting with spyware tailored to those device’s specific characteristics. Ominously, many of these infections took place without any visible indication of tampering or other clues that might have alerted them to the compromise. Also ominous is the fact that the services of Discover-Tech appear to span multiple regions around the globe. It is not known at this time exactly which governments are capitalizing on these new capabilities, but if past evidence is any indication it seems highly likely that some proportion of them are abusing those capabilities to target individuals outside of strictly criminal or national security purposes.

The hacking of Al Jazeera with AdFection is part of a longstanding pattern: mercenary spyware attacks against the media. Journalists and newsrooms are a constant target for spyware attacks, and this latest case highlights how well-resourced operators consistently seek new ways to access their private, protected communications.

The use of spyware to target the media directly interferes with the ability of the free press to hold power to account. It also threatens the privacy of journalists’ sources, and can chill reporting. Foreknowledge of movements, reporting topics, meetings, and sources does not just help powerful interests try to frustrate coverage and reporting, it can put people at physical risk. This is especially true for a news organization with reporters, freelancers, stringers, fixers and sources working in conflict zones around the world.

Investigations into mercenary spyware operations have repeatedly surfaced targeting against the media, including in the context of governmental and cartel killings of reporters. Journalists have been confirmed spyware targets, from the Citizen Lab’s earliest findings of Pegasus spyware in Mexico almost a decade ago, to cases across Africa from Angola to Morocco and Togo, to Jordan, Serbia, El Salvador, and Italy, among many others. Organizations like Reporters Without Borders provide helpful overviews of the scale of the threat which, as Access Now points out, is sometimes coupled with laws designed to authorize government access to journalists’ communications. The International Federation of Journalists, meanwhile, has a recent overview of how spyware is situated within a broader set of digital threats against journalists.

Recently, reporting from the Committee to Protect Journalists outlined the dangers posed to journalists from ADINT-style tracking. The combination of this tracking with zero-click mercenary spyware targeting presents an even more serious danger to journalists’ safety.

This investigation should also serve as a clear warning signal to news organizations around the world that they may be being actively targeted via this new threat. This targeting may happen both in newsrooms and to individual journalists, editors, and other staff members. We urge news organizations to immediately seek expert assistance and ensure that their systems are protected against these attacks to the fullest extent possible. We provide some guidance in Section 11, however we urge all news organizations to systematically review their security posture (and logs) for signs of AdFection style spyware targeting and infection.

Our findings also reveal a troubling lack of due diligence within the digital advertising industry that helped enable this inappropriate activity. Discover-Tech, which presented itself as a legitimate ad vendor but served as a bridge between the online advertising ecosystem and the spyware industry, has been deeply embedded and interconnected with the online advertising ecosystem for years. Multiple ad vendors let the company utilize their systems. The two key industry organizations, Google and IAB Europe, have helped Discover-Tech appear as a legitimate ad vendor from the year 2020 until 2026, despite information about the company’s links to figures in the spyware industry being readily accessible in corporate records. Our findings show that the digital advertising industry is ill-prepared to prevent malicious actors from exploiting its infrastructure for the distribution of spyware via targeted ads.

This case should serve as an alarm to the advertising industry that business as usual is no longer acceptable. The online advertising industry must get serious about tackling the distribution of mercenary spyware via targeted ads, alongside other malicious advertising practices including financially motivated fraud and cybercrime. Technical and organizational measures currently implemented by the industry, such as the SafeFrame specification or standards for supply chain transparency are insufficient or not even adopted in a meaningful way.

More broadly, the distribution of spyware via targeted ads depends on the way digital advertising – and the web economy at large – currently operate.

Many mobile apps and websites contain tracking software operated by dozens of third parties, which themselves may include code by additional third parties within apps and browsers. Also required for the targeted deployment of spyware, ad targeting at the individual level depends on uncontrolled data sharing via RTB auctions and third-party tracking.

Automated ad selling and buying via RTB, which connects large numbers of publishers, advertisers and intermediaries across opaque supply chains, is designed to minimize human intervention. When combined with a lack of oversight and accountability, it is generally prone to abuse. This is further aggravated by the assumption that at least some ad vendors benefit from malicious and fraudulent advertising. Leaked internal documents from Meta reported by Reuters suggest that Meta estimated that it earns between five and ten percent of its annual revenue from running fraudulent ads. Industry sources suggest that ad fraud accounts for one fifth of all online advertising spend.

This broken digital infrastructure needs to be reformed at several levels, as consumer associations, regulators, and policymakers have long been demanding.

The distribution of spyware via targeted ads represents a security risk not only for potential victims but also for states and civil society at large. Two major U.S. security agencies, the National Security Agency (NSA) and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA), have warned already in 2018 and 2020 that adversaries may leverage malicious ads to deploy malware on devices, and thus both recommended that government agencies and other organizations use ad-blocking software.

Given the current threat posed by Discover-Tech’s AdFection vectors, and the evidence of wide-scale targeting, we judge that the most feasible protection is for defenders to block targeted ads at the gateway. This defensive recommendation (see Section 11) holds until the industry has shown that it is reliably able to block all AdFection style vectors.

At the very time that state actors may be employing offensive cyber attacks, malicious ads can be deployed via apps and websites used by defense personnel, political leaders, and people maintaining critical infrastructure alike, creating national security risks for those very same states. The same structural deficits that endanger civil society, journalists, and opposition figures are potentially exploited by both foreign adversaries and cybercriminals, creating systemic risks for everyone. These security risks make it apparent that there is an urgent public-interest need to reform digital advertising.

The same risks apply to the private sector and to civil society. Indeed, as prior research has made clear, a large number of governments will use these potent capabilities to undermine political opposition, stealthily target journalists and lawyers, and target refugees, immigrants, and other vulnerable populations. The mercenary spyware industry is already notorious for widespread harms; fueling that industry with digital advertising capabilities will multiply those harms immeasurably.

The AdFection attacks and espionage described in this report impact millions of people in dozens of countries. Existing laws and self-regulation by the industry failed to catch or prevent them. In this section, we provide guidance to regulators, defenders, and the advertising industry on how to stop AdFection and ADINT-style espionage.

The advertising industry uses terms like “certified” and “approved” to try and convey a veneer of effective self regulation. However, the industry appears to perform no meaningful due diligence on participating vendors, instead improperly relying on self-attestation where vendors check a box on an online form. This process allows widespread privacy abuses, including failing to prevent mass espionage via targeted ads.

Ad vendors must significantly level up their cybersecurity and threat detection capacity to effectively cut off malicious advertisers across the supply chain. They must rigorously and regularly vet, screen, and audit their business partners and hold them accountable for their own supply chains. This type of more robust due diligence applies in particular to key industry organizations and dominant players who must introduce rigorous and regular audits for companies listed in ad vendor registries which they maintain and provide to many other actors in the supply chain. Business partners from countries with opaque corporate registries or where known malicious actors operate deserve specific attention.

Technical and organizational measures to be taken must include both vendor-specific and industry-wide efforts. Cybersecurity agencies and other regulators in the U.S., Canada, Europe, and other regions must support these efforts by investigating risks, calling out shortcomings and taking action to ensure the implementation of effective measures by the advertising industry.

We urge regulators to take immediate action to ensure that advertising platforms and partners stop facilitating AdFection-style attacks, and secure their populations from the security, cybersecurity, and privacy threats posed by the advertising ecosystem.

AdFection attacks demonstrate that online advertising is now a vector for zero-click spyware infection into your organization. Taken together with research showing that data from targeted advertising is already being used for mass espionage, and potentially for corporate espionage, this makes it clear there is currently no consistently safe way to expose your users and networks to targeted ads. You can directly block Discover-Tech’s current methods by blocking advertising identifiers, however we suspect that the AdFection attack surface may be larger, requiring more systematic measures.

AdFection is a complex threat, and if you face elevated risk because of who you are or what you do, we strongly recommend seeking expert help. However, there are certain actions you can take to reduce some AdFection risks.

Our investigation found that an attacker that we call DARK CARTOGRAPHER used Discover-Tech ads and a number of additional vendors to deanonymize users at scale since at least 2019. As these efforts rely on the exploitation of widespread security issues across numerous mobile providers, disclosure to providers is in progress. We will release a subsequent report delving into technical analysis and attribution of these attacks once the disclosure process is complete.

Google dominates the digital advertising ecosystem in the U.S., Europe, and other regions. It operates a massive ad exchange and systems for ad sellers (Ad Manager, AdSense, AdMob) and ad buyers (Google Ads, DV360). Its “Authorized Buyers” program allows third-party ad vendors to deliver ads by participating in ad auctions on Google’s ad exchange.

Yandex, although much smaller in revenue, similarly dominates the digital advertising ecosystem in Russia and some other regions. It also provides both an ad exchange and systems for ad sellers and buyers.

Beeswax is a major US-based ad buying platform, since 2021 owned by Comcast’s ad platform FreeWheel. It offers a Demand-Side Platform (DSP) that helps advertisers and other ad vendors deliver targeted ads to users by participating in ad auctions. Its “bidder-as-a-service” product is considered highly customizable and imposes fewer restrictions on its clients than other DSPs.

The FreeWheel website states that, by using Beeswax’ ad buying platform rather than other DSPs, clients could “access the full, unfiltered stream of RTB events, in much the same way [they] would if [they] were building a bidder from scratch”. Clients can augment the stream of ad bidding data they receive, for example, by “mapping” users to “rich profiles”, and they can use custom bidding algorithms and targeting attributes.

While this appears to offer great flexibility to clients to an extent that may come close to operating their own DSP, FreeWheel takes care of the integrations with ad exchanges and Supply-Side Platforms (SSPs) that help app and website publishers sell ads. As of July 2026, the FreeWheel website lists integrations with 36 “supply partners” including Google, Amazon, Microsoft, Index Exchange, and many others.

Beeswax is listed as an approved TCF ad vendor by IAB Europe (vendor list). Google lists Beeswax as a certified ad vendor and among its “common” European ad technology partners which Google will use by default when publishers do not set up a custom list of ad vendors. For its ad serving and third-party tracking, Beeswax uses the domain bidr[.]io and the cookie identifier bito (devicedisclosure.json).

Eskimi is a digital advertising group based in Lithuania with offices in Greece, Turkey, Japan, United Arab Emirates, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Nigeria, and Kenya, according to its website, eskimi.com. Its ad buying platform Eskimi DSP, which allows its clients to target 1.5 billion “profiled users” across 60 ad exchanges, according to the company, is also offered as a “white-label” version that “enables agencies, ad networks, and businesses to offer ‘Eskimi DSP’ under their own brand”. Eskimi also provides a data management platform (DMP) that “collects and stores data” it receives from 50 ad exchanges, amounting to two2 billion profiles, according to a 2025 version of the company’s website. Its website and Lithuanian company records show that it is incorporated as “UAB Eskimi”, also known as “UAB Aktyvus sektorius”.

Eskimi is much lesser known than Beeswax. Except for two paid posts, we did not find any articles discussing the company on digital advertising trade press sites like Adweek, Digiday, and AdExchanger. Eskimi was, however, prominently discussed when US-based data broker Datastream Group told U.S. Senator Ron Wyden that Eskimi was the source of 3.6 billion location data records revealing the exact movements of millions of people, including U.S. military and intelligence personnel, as reported in a joint investigation by German netzpolitik.org and other outlets. This investigation has helped spark extensive debates about ad surveillance.

While German netzpolitik.org found several additional links between the analyzed data and the company, Eskimi denied that it was the source of the data. Google told 404 Media that Eskimi is “part of Google’s Authorized Buyer program and must abide by our policies”. It added that it “regularly audits its Authorized Buyers program participants”. Eskimi is closely linked to the location data broker Redmob, which claims to sell data on one billion people across 150 countries according to its website, redmob.io. While Redmob is incorporated in Dubai, netzpolitik.org found that Eskimi and Redmob share the same CEO, who responded to their questions about Eskimi from a Redmob email address.

As of July 2026, Eskimi is listed as an approved TCF ad vendor by IAB Europe (vendor list). Google lists Eskimi as a certified ad vendor and among its European ad technology partners.

Vungle was a mobile advertising firm that merged with the U.S.-based mobile advertising firm Liftoff, which went public in June 2026. Since the merger, Liftoff offers several Vungle-branded products including a Supply-Side Platform (SSP) named Monetize, which helps app publishers sell ads, and the mobile ad exchange Vungle Exchange, which helps marketers buy ads served in mobile apps.

Both the SSP and the ad exchange rely on the Vungle SDK, which is a piece of advertising and tracking software embedded in many Android, iOS, Amazon, Windows, and Unity apps. The Vungle SDK is embedded in 150,000 mobile apps used by one billion people across 150 countries, which also describes the number of users that can be targeted via the Vungle ad exchange, according to the company.

Guidelines for the Vungle ad exchange contain a rule that asks clients to “refrain from” using the platform for the distribution of “malware, spyware, and files that can harm or gain unauthorized access to a device or user information”. We did not find an explanation of how the company monitors and enforces this rule.

Vungle has been controversially discussed in several papers and reports on mobile tracking and privacy. The Norwegian Consumer Council found in 2020 that Vungle received GPS coordinates and other personal data on users of Grindr and another mobile app, seemingly without a legal basis under the GDPR.

As of July 2026, Liftoff’s “Monetize” and “Vungle Exchange” products are listed as approved TCF ad vendors by IAB Europe (vendor list). Google lists Liftoff’s DSP and Monetize products as certified ad vendors and it lists Liftoff among its “common” European ad technology partners that Google will use by default when publishers do not choose a custom list of ad vendors.

Google has been deeply interconnected with Vungle from its inception. Google Ventures was an investor in Vungle’s seed, series A, and series B funding rounds. The Norwegian Consumer Council pointed out in 2020 that Google’s mobile advertising system AdMob “provides Vungle with access to extra features that allow Vungle to bypass data filters, and thus send more data to its partners than what would ordinarily be possible through Google’s regular advertising tools”. As of July 2026, Liftoff’s Vungle product Monetize is listed among a few “premium bidding partners” in Google’s mobile advertising system AdMob and among a few “ad sources” for AdMob’s advertising services on Android and iOS.

The site also refers to the company as “Shunfei Technology”. The link to Sunteng’s DSP offering leads site visitors to biddingx.com (“BiddingX”), an entity that promotes itself as China’s largest DSP. Sunteng appears to operate also under the brand Bidex (bidex.cn), which focuses on “overseas programmatic”, i.e. on digital advertising services for non-Chinese clients. We assume that Sunteng, Shunfei, Bidex and BiddingX are part of the same Chinese group of companies with offices in Singapore and the US. Sunteng claims to process 50 billion ad bid requests a day across 10,000 mobile apps and 60 ad vendor partners, and it lists Eskimi as a partner.

While Microsoft shut down Xandr’s ad buying system, the “Invest” DSP, in early 2026, it continues to offer Xandr’s ad selling system, the “Monetize” SSP. Ad buyers who used the former Xandr DSP were “handed” to Amazon DSP, according to trade press reporting.

As shown in Section 6, Microsoft’s user ID syncing in the browser via the domain adnxs[.]com, which assigns a Microsoft user ID to people who visit the sites of ad sellers and maps it to user IDs assigned by other ad vendors, appears to remain operational as of June 2026. Xandr has long been operating massive identity databases. In 2020, when Xandr was still owned by AT&T, it reportedly operated an identity graph linking 5 billion identifiers.

As of July 2026, Microsoft’s ad system Xandr is listed as an approved TCF ad vendor by IAB Europe (vendor list). Google’s list of certified ad vendors contains four records for Xandr. Google also lists Xandr among its “common” European ad technology partners which Google will use by default when publishers do not choose a custom list of ad vendors.

Adtech vendor, ad vendor. Advertising technology intermediary such as a Demand-Side Platform (DSP), Supply-Side Platform (SSP) (both defined below) or ad exchange.

Ad Slot. Designated space or position on a website or mobile app reserved to display an ad.

Demand-Side Platform (DSP). System operated by an adtech intermediary that helps advertisers buy ad placements across many different websites or mobile apps in an automated way by participating in real-time auctions hosted by ad exchanges.

Supply-Side Platform (SSP). System operated by an adtech intermediary that helps publishers of websites or mobile apps sell ad slots in an automated way by participating in real-time auctions hosted by an ad exchange, which is often operated by the same ad vendor as the SSP.

Ad Exchange. Automated marketplace operated by an adtech intermediary that hosts real-time auctions which facilitate the selling of ad slots and the buying of ad placements across many publishers, advertisers and intermediaries like DSPs and SSPs. Ad exchanges are often operated by SSPs.

Real-Time Bidding (RTB). Automated high-frequency auctions hosted by ad exchanges where advertisers (or DSPs on their behalf) bid on ad placements offered by website and mobile app publishers (or their SSPs). When a user visits a website or uses an app that sells targeted ads via RTB, the publisher’s SSP initiates a bid request that transmits data about the user and the ad slot to several DSPs, who submit bids on behalf of advertisers. The ad exchange determines the winner of the auction and pushes the ad to the user.

Bid Request. RTB auction record that describes an ad slot and the user who currently visits a website or uses a mobile app. Bid requests are initiated by publishers and sent via an SSP and an ad exchange to several DSPs, which place bids in order to show ads to specific users on behalf of advertisers. Bid requests typically contain personal data about users in order to facilitate targeted advertising.

Mobile Advertising ID (MAID). Unique identifier for a mobile device used for advertising and tracking purposes, assigned by the device’s operating system such as Google Android or Apple iOS. While users can reset or delete mobile ad IDs in the settings, they are activated by default. Advertising and data companies use mobile ad IDs to link user data across contexts and vendors in order to track, follow, profile and target users.

Cookie ID. Unique identifier for a user’s web browser, typically stored and retrieved in the browser by third-party code operated by adtech vendors during website visits.
